Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verses 1–4:

﴿Blessed﴾ from al-barakah (blessing). It is a verb specific to Allah the Exalted, and it has no present-tense form. ﴿upon His servant﴾ meaning Muhammad ﷺ, and this is in a manner of honouring him and singling him out. ﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾. The pronoun refers to Muhammad ﷺ or to the Qur'an, and the first is more apparent. His saying "to the worlds" is a general term that includes the jinn and mankind who were in his time and those who come after him until the Day of Resurrection. Creation (al-khalq) is an expression for bringing into existence after non-existence. Determination (al-taqdir) is an expression for perfecting the making, and assigning to each created thing its measure, its attributes, its time, its place, its benefit, its term, and other things. ﴿And they have taken﴾. The pronoun refers to Quraysh and others who associated partners with Allah the Exalted. ﴿And others helped him in it﴾. They mean a group of the Jews among them: ʿAddas, Yasar, and Abu Fukayhah al-Rumi. ﴿Then they have certainly produced an injustice and a falsehood﴾. That is, they wronged the Prophet ﷺ in what they attributed to him, and lied about him in that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 5:

﴿And they say: "Legends of the former peoples, which he has had written down, so they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ That is, what the ancients recorded in their books. The one who made this statement was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. ﴿Ikhtatabaha﴾ means that a scribe wrote them down for him, and then they were dictated to him so that he might memorize them. This is a report of the words of the disbelievers. Al-Hasan said: they are part of God's speech, in the form of a rebuttal to them. Had that been the case, it would have been said "a'ktatabaha" with a hamza at the beginning, for the meaning of denial. The hamza may be dropped in such a case. According to al-Hasan's view, one should pause at "asatir al-awwalin" (legends of the former peoples).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 6:

﴿Say: "He who knows the secret [of the heavens and the earth] has sent it down."﴾ This is a reply to the disbelievers in their saying [that the Qur'an is mere fabrication]. By "the secret" is meant what the disbelievers conceal of their sayings. Or it may be by way of disassociation and clearing oneself of what the disbelievers attributed to him of fabrication: that is, God knows my inner self, so He is the One who knows that I did not fabricate against Him; rather, He sent it down to me. If it is asked: what is the connection of His saying, ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ to what precedes it? The answer is that when He mentioned the sayings of the disbelievers, He followed them with this, to show that He is Forgiving and Merciful in that He did not hasten to punish them but gave them respite, and that if they embrace Islam, He will accept their repentance and forgive them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verses 7–10:

﴿And they say, "What is with this Messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ (the verse): This statement was made by the Quraysh as a means of disparaging the Prophet (ﷺ). Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they [too] ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]. Their saying ﴿this Messenger﴾ may be meant in the manner of their gods, like Pharaoh's saying: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 27]; or they may mean "the Messenger" according to his own claim. Then He mentioned the matters they proposed in their saying: ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ and what follows it. Then He described them with wrongdoing. We have already mentioned the meaning of "bewitched" (maskhur) in surah al-Isra' [47]. ﴿They have struck for you the examples﴾, i.e., they said those statements about you. ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾, i.e., they cannot reach the truth, because of their distance from it and their excessive ignorance. ﴿Better than that﴾: the reference is to what the disbelievers mentioned of treasure and a garden in this world. ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: meaning the gardens of the Hereafter and its palaces. It was also said: it means gardens and palaces in this world, and for this reason He said: "if He wills."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verses 13–14:

﴿مَكَاناً ضَيِّقاً﴾ "A narrow place," (they will be constrained) so that it becomes tighter upon them, as an increase in their punishment. ﴿مُّقَرَّنِينَ﴾ "Bound together": that is, some of them are tied to others. It is related that this is with chains of fire.

﴿دَعَوْاْ هُنَالِكَ ثُبُوراً﴾ "They will call out there for destruction." Ath-thubur (destruction): woe; and it is said: ruin. The meaning of their calling out "thubur" is that they say, "O thubura!" (O destruction!), like the speaker's saying, "Woe is me!" (wa-hasratah) and "Alas!" (wa-asafah).

﴿لاَّ تَدْعُواْ ٱلْيَوْمَ ثُبُوراً وَاحِداً﴾ "Do not call out today for one destruction." Its implied sense: it is said to them this, or their state requires it, even if there is no actual speech. Rather, they call out for many destructions, because their punishment is perpetual, so destruction renews upon them at every moment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verses 15–17:

﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity?"﴾ The comparison (tafdil) between the Garden and the Fire is permitted here because the speech is a question and a rebuke. Comparison is prohibited only between two things that share no common meaning when the speech is a statement. ﴿A promise that is asked for﴾: that is, requested by the believers or by the angels in their saying, "And admit them to the Gardens of Eternity." It was also said that it means a promise that must occur, because He has decreed it. ﴿Then He will say, "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray, or did they stray from the way themselves?"﴾ The one who says this is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and those addressed are those who were worshipped besides Allah, in general. It was also said that it refers specifically to the idols, but the first view is more preferred, because of His saying: ﴿Then He will say to the angels, "Did these people worship you?"﴾ [Saba' 34:40] and His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:116]. ﴿Or did they themselves stray from the way?﴾ Here "am" (or) is a counterpart (mu'adalah) to what precedes it. The meaning is that Allah says on the Day of Resurrection to those who were worshipped: "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray, or did they go astray", by their own accord and choice, and you did not lead them astray? For this reason He clarified this meaning by His saying: ﴿They﴾, so that the attribution of straying to them is established. Allah asked them this question, although He knows all matters, in order to rebuke the disbelievers who worshipped them.

The ones who say this are the ones who were worshipped. They said it to disown those who worshipped them, like their saying: "You are our guardian, not them." The purpose of this is to rebuke the disbelievers on that Day and to establish the proof against them.

﴿وَلَـٰكِن مَّتَّعْتَهُمْ وَآبَآءَهُمْ﴾ Its meaning: their being given enjoyment of blessings in this world was the cause of their forgetting the remembrance of God and His worship.

﴿قَوْماً بُوراً﴾ That is, perishing. It derives from *al-bawar* (البوار), which is destruction. Scholars differed over whether *bur* (بوراً) is the plural of *ba'ir* (بائر), or a verbal noun (masdar) used as a descriptive, which is why it can apply to the singular and the plural.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 19:

﴿So they have indeed denied you in what you say﴾. This is an address which God directed to the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection, meaning: your deities which you worshipped besides God have denied you, and disowned you. It is said: it is an address to the worshipped ones, meaning: they denied you in this statement when they were worshipped by you in the world. It is also said: it is an address to the Muslims, meaning: the disbelievers have denied you concerning what you say of tawhid (divine oneness) and the sharia (sacred law). It is also read as ﴿bima yaqulun﴾ with the yaʼ (third person) from below, and the bāʼ in His words ﴿bima taqulun﴾ (with what you say) on the reading with the tāʼ (second person) is a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿kadhdhabukum﴾ (they denied you). On the reading with the yāʼ it is like your saying: "I wrote with the pen," or: they denied you with their statement. ﴿Fa-ma tastatiʻuna sarfan wa-la nasran﴾ (so you cannot avert [the punishment] nor gain help). It is read as ﴿fa-ma tastatiʻuna﴾ with the tāʼ on top (second person). On this reading it is possible that the address is to the polytheists or to the worshipped ones; and "sarf" on these two possibilities means averting the punishment from them. Or the address is to the Muslims, and on this "sarf" means repelling the denial. It is also read with the yāʼ, and then it is attributed to the worshipped ones or to the polytheists, and "sarf" means the averting of the punishment. ﴿Wa-man yazlim minkum﴾ (and whoever among you does wrong): it is an address to the disbelievers; it is also said to be to the believers; and it is also said to be general.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 20:

﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they surely ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ Its implied meaning: "And We did not send before you messengers or men." On this reading, the omitted object is what the pronoun refers to in His words ﴿except that they surely ate food﴾. This verse is a rebuttal of the disbelievers who found it strange that a messenger should eat food and walk in the markets. ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾ This is addressed to all people, because of the difference in their conditions: the rich is a trial for the poor, the healthy is a trial for the sick, and the messenger is a trial for others who envy him and disbelieve in him. ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ Its implied meaning: "so that We may see whether you will be patient."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 21:

﴿Those who do not hope for Our meeting﴾. It was said: its meaning is "those who do not fear." The correct view is that it retains its original meaning, because the meeting with Allah is both hoped for and feared. ﴿"Why have not the angels been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?"﴾ The disbelievers proposed the descent of the angels or the sight of Allah, and that, they said, would make them believe. Allah answered them with His words: ﴿They have certainly been arrogant within themselves﴾, the verse. That is: they asked for what they had no right to ask for. As for His words ﴿within themselves﴾, it is like saying: "So-and-so is great in himself," meaning in his own estimation; or it means that they concealed disbelief within their own selves.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 22:

﴿On the day they see the angels, there will be no good news that day for the guilty.﴾ When they asked to see the angels, God informed them that there would be no good news for them on the day they see them. So the governing word (al-'amil) for "yawm" (day) is the phrase "lā bushrā" (there is no good news). "Yawma'idhin" (that day) is a substitute (badal) [for "yawm"], and ﴿and they will say, "[It is] a forbidding, forbidden [barrier]."﴾ If the pronoun in "yaqūlūna" (they say) refers to the angels, the meaning is that they say to the guilty, "ḥijran maḥjūran" (a forbidding, forbidden barrier), that is, "Paradise or good news is forbidden to you." If the pronoun refers to the guilty, the meaning is that they say "ḥijran" in the sense of "ʿawdhan" (a seeking of refuge). This is because the Arabs used to seek refuge with this word from what they disliked, and its accusative case is due to a verb whose expression is omitted, as in "ma'ādha Allāh" (God forbid).

"And We will proceed to what they did" (﴿وَقَدِمْنَآ إِلَىٰ مَا عَمِلُواْ﴾): meaning, We intended their deeds. The word "qudūm" (coming/arriving) is used figuratively. It was also said: it is the coming of the angels, which Allah attributed to Himself because it was by His command.

"And We made it scattered dust" (﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهُ هَبَآءً مَّنثُوراً﴾): an expression for the non-acceptance of the good deeds they did, such as feeding the poor, maintaining family ties, and other things, and that these will not benefit them, because faith is a condition for the acceptance of deeds. Al-habāʾ (هباء) are the fine particles of dust that are only visible when sunlight enters a narrow place such as a kuwwa (an opening, like a window). Al-manthūr means the scattered.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 24:

﴿Better in abode﴾ Here the comparison is made between Paradise and Hellfire, since both are places of settling (mustaqarr), though one is better than the other. ﴿And better in resting place﴾ The word maqil is of the pattern mif'al, from the noun of the midday rest (al-qa'ila), although there is no sleep in Paradise. It came in accordance with what the Arabs know of resting at the time of midday in cool places. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 25:

﴿And the Day the sky is split open with clouds﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection. The splitting of the sky (inshiqaq al-sama') is its cleaving asunder (infitar), and the meaning of "with clouds" (bil-ghamam) is that clouds emerge from it, namely the thin white clouds (al-sahab al-raqiq al-abyad). At that time the angels descend to the earth.

﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy﴾. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 32–33:

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾ This is among the objections of the Quraysh, for they said, "If the Qur'an were from Allah, it would have been sent down all at once, just as the Torah and the Gospel were sent down." ﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ This is the answer to them, and its meaning is: We sent it down in this manner, in installments, so that We might strengthen thereby the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) for memorizing it. Had it been sent down all at once, it would have been impossible for him to memorize it, because he was unlettered and could not read. Memorizing it in installments was therefore easier for him. Furthermore, it was sent down in response to various occasions (asbab), which require that each part of it be revealed when its occasion arises. Also, there is abrogation (naskh) and the abrogated (mansukh), and this cannot occur in what is sent down all at once. ﴿And We have recited it in measured recitation﴾ That is, We divided it into parts, separating it out, for it was sent down over a period of twenty years. ﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell﴾ means the disbelievers. Their being gathered upon their faces is literal, because a hadith has come about it. It was said that God sent them a prophet, and they threw him into a well, so God destroyed them. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 45:

﴿Have you not considered your Lord﴾, i.e., consider the workmanship and power of your Lord, ﴿how He extends the shade﴾. It has been said: it is the extension from the break of dawn until the rising of the sun, because the shade is then over the whole earth. Ibn 'Atiyyah (Ibn ʿAṭiyyah) objected to this, since that time belongs to the night, and one does not say "shade" (ẓill) at night. He chose that the extension of the shade is from the brightening (al-isfar) until the rising of the sun, and shortly after its setting. It has also been said: the meaning of "extends the shade" is that He makes it stretch out and spread. ﴿And had He willed, He would have made it still﴾, i.e., constant and not passing away, but He made it pass away by means of the sun. It has also been said: the meaning of "still" is not spread out upon the earth, but rather clinging to the base of a wall, a tree, and the like. ﴿Then We made the sun a guide for it﴾. It has been said: the meaning is that people are guided by the sun and its conditions, in its course over the shade: when it expands and when it contracts, and when it moves from one place to another; and they build upon that their benefit from it and their sitting in it. It has also been said: the meaning is that without the sun, it would not be known that the shade is a thing, because things are only known by their opposites.

Then We withdraw it to Us, withdrawing it gradually.

Its withdrawal is its abrogation (naskh) and its removal by the sun; and "gradually" (yasiran) means little by little, not all at once. If it is asked: what is the meaning of "then" (thumma) in these three places? The answer is that it may indicate sequence in time, that is, God made these states one after another; or it may indicate the gradation of these three states, that the second is greater than the first, and the third greater than the second.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verses 47–49:

﴿The night as a garment﴾: He likened the darkness of the night to a garment, because it covers everything as a garment does. ﴿And sleep as rest﴾: It was said: rest. And it was said: death, based on His words: ﴿It is Allah who takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]. What supports this is that sleep is contrasted with resurrection (nushur). ﴿The winds as heralds of good news﴾: This was mentioned in al-A'raf [7:57]. ﴿Pure water﴾: an intensive form of "tahir" (pure). It was also said: its meaning is purifying for people in wudu' and other than it. In this sense the jurists say: "pure water" (ma' tahur), meaning purifying (mutahhir), and everything purifying is pure, but not everything pure is purifying. ﴿And many of the cattle and people﴾: It was said: it is the plural of insi (human), and it was said: the plural of insan, and the first is more correct.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 53:

﴿مَرَجَ ٱلْبَحْرَيْنِ﴾ [He let loose the two seas]. People differed over this verse, because it is not known in this world that there is a salt sea and a sweet sea; the well-known seas are salt water. Ibn ʿAbbas said: by the salt sea, al-ujaj (the bitter, brackish), he meant the sea of the earth, and by the sweet sea, al-furat (the fresh), he meant the sea of the clouds. It was also said: the salt sea is the well-known sea, and the sweet sea is the waters of the earth. It was also said: the salt sea is all salt water, from wells and other sources, and the sweet sea is the waters of the earth, from rivers and springs. The meaning of "sweet" (ʿadhb) is that which has reached full sweetness to the point of inclining toward sweetness, and al-ajaj (bitter, brackish) is its opposite. The meaning of their "letting loose" (maraja) has been disputed: it was said that He made them adjacent and side by side, and it was said that He caused one of them to flow into the other. ﴿وَجَعَلَ بَيْنَهُمَا بَرْزَخاً وَحِجْراً مَّحْجُوراً﴾ [And He placed between them a barrier and a forbidding partition], meaning a separator between them, which is the land between them such that they do not mix. It was also said: the barrier is something God knows and humans do not see.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verses 54–55:

﴿He created man from water﴾. If by "man" (al-bashar) he means Adam, then "water" refers to the water with which he was created along with the earth, so it became clay (tin). If by "man" he means the descendants of Adam, then "water" refers to the semen (al-maniy) from which they are created. ﴿So He made him into lineage and marriage-relationship﴾. Nasab (lineage) and sihr (marriage-relationship, al-sihr) encompass every kind of kinship: that is, every relationship. Nasab is when a person and another share a father or a mother, whether near or distant. Sihr is the mixing that comes through marriage. It was also said: by nasab is meant the males, i.e., those of lineage to whom one is traced, and by sihr is meant the females, i.e., those through whom one becomes related by marriage. This is like His saying: ﴿And He made of it the two mates, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. ﴿And the disbeliever is ever an assistant against his Lord﴾. "The disbeliever" here refers to the category (al-jins). It was also said that the intended person is Abu Jahl. Al-zahir (the assistant) means the one who helps, i.e., he helps Satan against his Lord through enmity and polytheism. Its wording applies to the singular and the plural, like His saying: ﴿And the angels thereafter are supporters﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾, meaning: I do not ask you for any wage or benefit for faith. ﴿except for him who wills to take a way to his Lord﴾, meaning: I only ask you to take a way to your Lord through charity. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verses 58–59:

﴿And put your trust in the Ever-Living who does not die﴾. Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) recited this verse and said: "It is not fitting for anyone of intellect, after this, to place his trust in a creature, for it will die." ﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾. That is, say: "Glory be to God and praise be to Him." Tasbih (glorification) is declaring Him free of everything that does not befit Him. As for "with His praise," the meaning is: I say this together with His praise. It is also possible that the meaning is: glorify Him while accompanied by His praise, so it is a command to combine tasbih and hamd (praise). ﴿And sufficient is He as one who is Aware of the sins of His servants﴾. It may be that what is meant is the vastness of His forbearance and pardon toward His servants despite His knowledge of their sins, or it may be that what is meant is a warning to the servants, because God knows their sins. ﴿Then He istawa (rose) over the Throne﴾. This was mentioned in al-A'raf [7:54]. ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ is a predicate of an omitted subject (khabar mubtada' mudmar), or a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in istawa. ﴿So ask about Him one who is aware﴾. In this there are two meanings. The first, which is the more apparent: that what is meant is, "Ask about Him someone who is aware of Him and knowledgeable about Him," and khabiran (aware) is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul). This knowledgeable one who is asked is Jibril (peace be upon him), the scholars, and the People of the Book. The preposition ba' in His words ﴿bihi﴾ may be connected to khabiran, or may be connected to the asking, and its meaning in that case is the meaning of "an" (about). The second meaning: that what is meant is, "Ask by His asking one who is aware," i.e., if you ask Him, Exalted is He, you will find Him aware of everything, so khabiran is in the accusative of circumstance (hal). It is like your saying: "If you saw so-and-so, you would see a lion by seeing him," i.e., you would see by his sight a lion.

"They said, 'And what is the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)?'" When the Most Merciful was mentioned in the Qur'an, the Quraysh denied it and said, "We do not know the Most Merciful." Musaylima the Liar (al-Kadhdhab) had named himself al-Rahman, so they said, by way of sophistry: "The Rahman is only the man of al-Yamama." "Shall we prostrate to what you command us?" Its meaning: to what you command us to prostrate to. "And it increased them in aversion (nufur)." The pronoun object in "increased them" refers to the one spoken of, namely "Prostrate to the Most Merciful."

"Towers (buruj)" means the twelve mansions (manazil), and it is said [they are] the great stars. "A lamp (siraj)" means the sun. It has also been recited with a dammah on the sin and the ra', as "sural" (plural), meaning all lights. Then he specified the moon for mention, as an honour.

"He made the night and the day alternating (khilfa)": meaning one succeeds the other. It is also said that it is from ikhtilaf (difference), because this one is white and that one is black. Khilfa is a noun of form, like rukba (a way of kneeling) and jilsa (a way of sitting), and the original sense is "He made them possessors of alternation."

"For whoever wishes to remember (an yadhdhakkara)": it is said its meaning is to take heed from the created things. It is also said its meaning is to remember what one has missed of the prayers and other acts in the night, so that one makes it up during the day, or what one has missed during the day, so that one makes it up at night. This is the view of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 63:

﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾: that is, His servants who are pleasing to Him; servanthood here is one of honour and dignity. ﴿And the servants﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, or His saying at the end of the surah: ﴿These will be rewarded with the high chamber﴾ [al-Furqan: 75] ﴿those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾: that is, gently and softly, with forbearance and dignified calm. It may be that this describes the manner of their walking upon the earth, or describes their character in all their conditions, and walking upon the earth is used to express all their conduct during their lifetime. ﴿They say: "Peace (salaman)"﴾: that is, they speak a sound, right word, so as to repel the ignorant gently. It was also said that its meaning is: they say to the ignorant, "Peace," meaning this very word, in the sense of "We are free of you (salimna minkum)." Some of them said: this verse is abrogated by the sword, and abrogation is valid only with regard to the disbelievers; as for overlooking the foolish and showing forbearance towards them, it is commendable and not abrogated.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 65:

﴿Indeed, its punishment is ever a continual torment﴾ and what follows it may be either from their words or from the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Ever a continual torment﴾ means destruction and ruin (halak wa khasaran). It has also been said that it means "constant, clinging to them" (mulaziman).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 67:

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever between that (the middle course)﴾ — Al-iqtar (stinginess, niggardliness) is restriction in spending and miserliness (al-shuhh), and its opposite is al-israf (extravagance, wastefulness). He forbade both extremes and commanded moderation between them, which is al-qiwam (the balanced middle course). This applies to spending on what is permissible and on acts of obedience. As for spending on acts of disobedience, it is extravagance, even if it is little.

﴿And whoever does that will meet with a penalty (athām)﴾. That is, a punishment. It is also said: athām means sin (ithm), so the meaning is "he will meet the recompense of sin." And it is said: athām is a valley in Hell. The reference of "that" (dhālika) is to what was mentioned: associating partners with Allah, killing a soul without right, and fornication.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 69:

﴿And he will abide therein in humiliation﴾ It is said: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers, because they are the ones who abide forever in the Fire by consensus (ijma'). So it is as if He said: those who combine shirk (associating partners with God), killing and fornication. It is also said: it was revealed concerning the believers who kill a soul and commit fornication. As for the view of the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilite school), then "khulud" (abiding forever) is taken in its literal sense. As for the view of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah), then "khulud" is an expression for a long duration.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 70:

﴿Except for one who repents﴾ If we say the verse refers to disbelievers, then there is no difficulty in it, for when the disbeliever embraces Islam, his repentance from disbelief, killing and fornication is valid. If we say it refers to believers, there is no disagreement that repentance from fornication is valid, but there is disagreement over whether a Muslim's repentance from killing is valid or not. ﴿Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ It has been said: Allah will enable them to do good deeds in place of the evil deeds they committed. And it has been said: this replacement will take place in the Hereafter, i.e., the punishment for evil deeds will be replaced with the reward for good deeds.

﴿He turns back to Allah, a true turning-back﴾. That is, a repentance that is accepted and pleasing in the sight of Allah, just as you say: "You have indeed spoken a speech, O so-and-so," meaning a good speech.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 72:

﴿They do not bear false witness﴾. That is, they do not testify to falsehood (zur), which is lying, so it derives from testimony (shahada). It has also been said that the meaning is: they do not attend gatherings of falsehood and frivolity (lahw). According to this view, it is from witnessing (mushahada) and attending (hudur). The first view is more apparent. ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾. Lagha (idle talk) is ugly speech in its various kinds. The meaning of ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾ is that they turn away from it and feel shame, and do not enter into it along with its people, in order to keep themselves pure of that.

﴿They do not fall down upon them deaf and blind﴾. That is, they do not turn away from the signs of Allah; rather, they turn toward them with their ears and their hearts. So the negation applies to deafness and blindness, not to falling down upon them.

Qurrata a'yunin (coolness of eyes). It was said: its meaning is, "Make our spouses and our offspring obedient to You." And it was said: "Admit them with us into Paradise." The wording is more general than that.

﴿And grant us, [as] leaders for the righteous.﴾ That is, exemplars whom the righteous may follow. Imaman (leader) is singular but is meant as a collective noun (jins). It was also said that it is a plural of amm, meaning "one who follows."

﴿The chamber﴾: meaning the chamber of Paradise. It is a noun of genus (ism jins).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 25, verse 77:

﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication.﴾ It is possible that "mā" here is a negation or an interrogative. There are three opinions regarding the meaning of "du'ā'" (supplication) here. The first: the meaning is that Allah does not care for you were it not for your worship of Him, so "du'ā'" means "ʿibādah" (worship). This is close to the meaning of His saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. The second: "du'ā'" means seeking help and asking, and the meaning is: Allah does not care for you, but He shows mercy to you when you seek help from Him and call upon Him. On these two opinions, the address is to all people, believers and disbelievers alike, because among them are those who worship Allah and call upon Him; or the address is to the believers specifically, because they are the ones who call upon Allah and worship Him. However, this is weakened by His saying: "for you have indeed denied." The third: the address is specifically to the disbelievers, and the meaning according to this is: My Lord would not care for you were it not that He calls you to His religion. On this view, "du'ā'" means the command to enter the religion, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) construed with its object; whereas on the first and second opinions it is a verbal noun construed with its subject. ﴿So you have indeed denied﴾: this is an address to the Quraysh and other disbelievers, not to the believers. ﴿So it will be inevitable (lizāman)﴾: that is, the punishment will be inevitable and certain. The punishment was left implicit, though it is the subject of "kāna" (will be), because it is the requital of the earlier denial. It is disputed whether "the punishment" here refers to the killing on the day of Badr or to the punishment of the Hereafter.
